title: Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935)
summary: The FTC Act limited removal to specified causes, and the Court upheld that protection for the commission as characterized in the opinion. Overruled by Trump v. Slaughter (2026).
notes: In Trump v. Slaughter, decided June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court held 6–3 that the FTC Act’s for-cause removal restriction violates Article II and overruled Humphrey’s Executor: “If anything more is left of Humphrey’s, we overrule it.” Read this brief as the 1935 holding and as the framework the later removal cases argued about, not as current law. The class 11 Slaughter supplement is assigned reading; open the Trump v. Slaughter entry for the decision.

sections.Parties: The executor of Federal Trade Commissioner William E. Humphrey challenged President Roosevelt’s removal of Humphrey. The United States argued that the President had constitutional authority to remove him despite the statutory grounds.
sections.Material Facts: President Hoover reappointed Humphrey for a seven-year term. Roosevelt requested his resignation because the administration wanted personnel whose policy views aligned with its own, while disclaiming criticism of Humphrey’s personal service. Humphrey refused, and Roosevelt removed him in October 1933. The FTC Act provided staggered terms, political-balance requirements, and removal for inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office. The government did not allege any listed cause.
sections.Procedural History: The case arose through certified questions concerning whether the statute limited removal to its named causes and whether that limitation was constitutional. The Court answered both questions affirmatively. The source records Humphrey’s assertion of continued office and compensation and later identifies the litigation as a back-pay claim; it does not reproduce a final monetary judgment.
sections.Issue: Did the listed grounds restrict removal of an FTC commissioner, and could Congress constitutionally impose that restriction?
sections.Holding: Yes. The statutory grounds were exclusive, and Roosevelt’s policy disagreement did not authorize removal. Congress could protect officers serving the commission’s quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial functions as the Court characterized them.
sections.Reasoning: The Court combined the statutory text, fixed tenure, institutional design, reports, and debates to identify an intended expert body exercising independent judgment. It read Myers narrowly as involving a purely executive postmaster and disapproved broader dicta that would defeat this protection. The commission’s investigatory, legislative-assistance, and adjudicatory duties supported a different constitutional treatment in this opinion. Independence would be insecure if an official held office entirely at another official’s pleasure. The Court expressly left intermediate cases for future consideration. Later assigned cases revised the functional vocabulary and debated the decision’s scope. Trump v. Slaughter (2026) has since overruled it.

topics.lrs-s-removal: For-cause protection was upheld for the commission as characterized by the Court; Trump v. Slaughter (2026) overruled that holding.
topics.lrs-s-agency-independence: Staggered terms, expert functions, political balance, and removal limits were evidence of intended independent judgment.
topics.lrs-s-statutory-context: The opinion used text, structure, and legislative history to treat the specified removal grounds as exclusive.
